title: Honest Baseline

learn.summary: You can't improve what you haven't measured. Four numbers give a surprisingly complete picture: resting heart rate, a timed 1-mile walk, max push-ups, and the 30-second sit-to-stand test. Record them once, honestly, before changing anything — they become your progress scoreboard.

do: This week, record all four baselines in your notes app: resting HR, 1-mile walk time, push-up max, and 30-second sit-to-stand count. Date the entry.

children.title: Resting Heart Rate

learn.summary: Measure first thing in the morning, before coffee, sitting quietly: count beats for 60 seconds at the wrist or neck. Most adults land between 60–100 bpm; well-trained people often sit in the 50s. A downward trend over months is one of the clearest signs your aerobic base is improving.

do: Measure your resting HR on 3 consecutive mornings this week and record the average.

children.title: Timed Walk Test

learn.summary: The Rockport 1-mile walk test estimates aerobic fitness with nothing but a flat mile and a watch: walk as fast as you can sustain, note the time and your heart rate at the finish. Under 15 minutes is a solid starting point for most adults; under 13 is good. The Cooper 12-minute run test is the harder cousin for when you're ready.

do: Walk 1 mile as fast as you comfortably can and record your time and finishing heart rate.

children.title: Push-Up Max Test

learn.summary: One unbroken set of push-ups, chest to within a fist of the floor, full lockout at the top — no sagging hips, no half reps. A 2019 study of firefighters found those who could do 40+ had dramatically lower cardiovascular risk than those under 10. Can't do a full push-up yet? Test from an elevated surface like a countertop and note the height.

do: Do one max-effort set of strict push-ups (or counter push-ups) today and record the number and variation.

children.title: Sit-to-Stand Test

learn.summary: The 30-second chair stand: arms crossed on chest, stand fully and sit back down as many times as possible in 30 seconds. It's a validated CDC/STEADI screen for leg strength and fall risk — under 12 reps for adults over 60 flags concern, while fit younger adults often exceed 20. It doubles as a brutal little leg workout.

do: Do the 30-second chair stand test today with a standard-height chair and record your rep count.
